intro: Vancouver's own heritage register tracks its remarkable trees by street address, not by park, and what turns up is civic survivors rather than old-growth giants: an oak that has held one corner of City Hall's lawn since the building opened, a magnolia pair the city rescued from a bulldozer, the widest Caucasian wingnut on Vancouver's street-tree books, and a run of thick-trunked beeches, chestnuts and oaks on ordinary residential streets. None carries a confirmed planting date older than about a century, and the register says so honestly.
meta_description: Vancouver's most remarkable trees: a City Hall oak, the city's widest Caucasian wingnut, and two magnolias rescued from a 1966 bulldozer.
question_meta: Vancouver's most specifically dated tree is a pair of 1912 magnolias in Vanier Park; an undated wingnut on Comox Street may be older. Full list of 7.
question_answer: Vancouver's most specifically dated remarkable tree is the pair of saucer magnolias at the H.R. MacMillan Space Centre in Vanier Park, planted in 1912 and about 114 years old. The Comox Street Caucasian wingnut, the widest of its kind on the city's own tree inventory, may be older still, but no record gives it an exact planting year.
question_context: Vancouver's heritage tree register is built from street addresses rather than a forest survey, so what it turns up are civic and institutional survivors: trees that outlasted the buildings or events around them rather than trees left standing in old growth. The magnolias at the Space Centre have the clearest paper trail of the seven, a documented 1912 planting outside the old Vancouver Court House, a rescue from destruction in 1966, and a 1968 replanting in Vanier Park by the Park Board. The Comox Street wingnut carries no planting date at all, only a trunk thick enough, at 116.8 centimetres across, to be the widest of 43 wingnuts on the city's own street-tree inventory, which argues for real age without proving it. City Hall's oak has two competing origin stories that disagree by nine years and do not both hold up, and the Normal School Red Oak outside City Square Mall has no story at all beyond its species and address. Three more come from the city's landscape-resources listing, a beech, a chestnut and an oak on residential boulevards, cross-checked against the city's own street-tree survey and none of them dated either. All seven are free to see.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Vancouver?
faq.a: No exact planting record survives for most of Vancouver's remarkable trees. The most specific date on record belongs to the pair of saucer magnolias in Vanier Park, planted in 1912. The Comox Street Caucasian wingnut, the widest of its kind on the city's own inventory, may be older, but nothing dates it precisely.

faq.q: Why aren't these old-growth rainforest trees?
faq.a: Vancouver's heritage tree register tracks remarkable trees by street address in the built city, not a survey of surviving old-growth forest. What it turns up is oaks on civic lawns, a mall courtyard and a street corner, not giants in a park reserve.

faq.q: Did King George really give City Hall its oak tree?
faq.a: Two sources disagree. One says a small oak was planted in 1936, the year City Hall opened. Another says King George presented it on a visit in 1945, but George VI's only trip to British Columbia was in 1939, and he never returned to Canada after the war. Nobody has settled which account is right.

faq.q: Are Vancouver's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes. All seven stand on public grounds or a public street: City Hall's lawn, the plaza of a shopping centre built around a former school, a West End street corner, the open forecourt of a museum whose building charges admission but whose grounds do not, and three residential boulevards in Kitsilano, Arbutus Ridge and Dunbar-Southlands.

trees.name: The City Hall Oak

location.neighbourhood: Mount Pleasant (Vancouver City Hall grounds, southwest corner)

trees.story:
Vancouver's heritage register lists this oak the way it lists buildings, and two accounts explain how it got there. They cannot both be right. Nature Vancouver's survey of the City Hall grounds says a small oak was planted in 1936, the year the building opened during the city's golden jubilee, and that it now fully occupies the southwest corner of the lawn. The Vancouver Heritage Foundation's page for the address says something else: that King George presented an oak on a visit in 1945. That version trips over its own date. George VI came to British Columbia once, on the royal tour of May 1939, and he did not travel to Canada again after the war. We have taken the 1936 planting as the likelier of the two, which puts the tree at about ninety, and anyone holding the paperwork that settles it should tell us.

The corner, at least, is not in dispute. City Hall went up in the depths of the Depression and opened in 1936 for the city's fiftieth birthday, and the oak has been filling its southwest corner through every argument the building has hosted since. Nobody has put a tape around the trunk. If you do, tell us what it reads.
verified_sources: https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/heritage-sites/ (record id 2523, heritage_register_id 2523, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, English Oak, 453 W 12TH AV, municipaldesignationm=No)
trees.access: Free. Stands on the public grounds of Vancouver City Hall; open daylight hours, no entry restriction.
trees.transport: Broadway-City Hall SkyTrain (Canada Line/Millennium Line), about 8 minute walk east along W 12th Ave.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, filling the southwest corner of the City Hall lawn. Nobody has ever put a tape around it.

trees.name: The Normal School Red Oak

location.address: 555 West 12th Avenue, Vancouver, BC (City Square Shopping Centre, at the former Provincial Normal School building; register address given as 501 W 12th Ave)

trees.story:
The city's heritage register carries one line about this tree: Northern Red Oak, 501 West 12th Avenue. No age, no girth, no account of who put it there, and nothing else written about it anywhere we have looked, which is unusual for a tree on a register at all. So take what follows as the address talking rather than the tree.

That address is the Provincial Normal School, built in 1908 and 1909, a normal school being a teacher training college; British Columbia sent its future schoolteachers here. The building was given municipal heritage protection in 1986, and in 1989 Paul Merrick Architects put a shopping centre around it rather than over it, which is why the school's brick front still faces West 12th from inside a mall called City Square. The oak stands out on the grounds, a minute from the Broadway-City Hall SkyTrain entrance and a short walk along the same street from City Hall's own listed oak, which makes the two of them one easy stop.

Quercus rubra is an eastern North American tree and did not reach this coast on its own, so somebody planted it on purpose. When, nobody appears to have recorded, and the school's dates are not an answer for the tree. If you know, tell us.

best_time.label: late October into November, when a red oak turns the deep red it is named for

verified_sources: https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/heritage-sites/ (record id 2522, heritage_register_id 2522, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, Northern Red Oak, 501 W 12TH AV, municipaldesignationm=No)
trees.access: Free. On the public plaza/grounds of City Square Shopping Centre, built around the preserved 1908-09 Provincial Normal School building. Open to the public as a commercial mall precinct.
trees.transport: Broadway-City Hall SkyTrain station is directly adjacent (City Square Mall sits on top of/beside it).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, on the grounds outside the old Normal School's brick front, now enclosed by the City Square mall. Nothing else about this tree has ever been recorded.

trees.name: The Comox Street Wingnut

location.address: 2020 Comox Street, Vancouver, BC (at Chilco Street, West End)

trees.story:
Vancouver's street tree inventory has 43 wingnuts on its books, and this one, on a residential corner in the West End, is the largest Caucasian wingnut among them. The city measured the trunk at 116.8 centimetres across, which is about 367 centimetres around, under a crown 13.7 metres up. The runner-up, out on Yew Street, is five centimetres narrower.

Pterocarya fraxinifolia is a walnut relative from the Caucasus and the forests along the Caspian in northern Iran, and it has one unmistakable trick. Through July and August it hangs chains of winged nutlets from the branch tips, green strings half a metre long, and on a street tree like this one they hang low enough to take in a hand. Out of season, look for the deeply furrowed trunk and the long compound leaves; from a distance a wingnut is easy to walk past as a big ash.

The Heritage Vancouver Society put it in a 2006 newsletter round-up of the city's heritage trees worth the walk, with its own photograph. Nobody has dated it. The trunk points to a century or more, but this genus puts on girth quickly, so a thick wingnut is not automatically an old one and the number should be held loosely. If the century is right, it kept this corner while the West End around it went from houses to apartment towers.

best_time.label: July and August, when half-metre chains of winged nutlets hang from every branch tip

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in summer by the half-metre chains of winged nutlets hanging from its branch tips, and year round by its deeply furrowed trunk. It stands on the Comox and Chilco corner.

trees.name: The Planetarium Magnolias

location.address: H.R. MacMillan Space Centre, 1100 Chestnut Street, Vanier Park, Vancouver, BC

trees.story:
These two magnolias spent two years parked in a landscape contractor's garden because he would not destroy them. In 1966 the province wanted the ground they stood on, outside the old Vancouver Court House downtown, for a new government fountain, and the pair was scheduled for disposal. The public objected loudly enough that the contractor hired to clear the site, K. Johnsen, moved the trees to his own property instead. In 1968 the Vancouver Park Board acquired them and replanted them in Vanier Park, flanking the two ramp entrances of what was then the H.R. MacMillan Planetarium and is now the Space Centre. The courthouse they were dug out of is today the Vancouver Art Gallery.

They went in as young trees in 1912, which puts them a little past a century; that figure comes from the recorded planting date rather than from anything measured on the trunk. A saucer magnolia is a hybrid raised outside Paris in the 1820s and named for the man who made it, Soulange-Bodin, and it flowers the way that reputation suggests: in late March and April, before a leaf appears, both trees fill with pink and white goblets on bare grey wood.

The rescue is set down in a 2006 Heritage Vancouver Society newsletter, the one detailed account of these trees we have found. The city register still lists them as a single line, and there are two of them, one at each ramp.

best_time.label: late March and April, when both trees flower pink and white on bare wood before the leaves

Heritage Vancouver Society Newsletter, Volume 15 Number 2, April/May 2006, 'Out on a Limb for Heritage', https://www.heritagevancouver.org/pdf_newsletter/hvs-news-2006-02-screen.pdf

trees.transport: Vanier Park, about a 15 minute walk from Granville Island or across the Burrard Bridge from downtown; bus #2 or #22 to Cornwall/Cypress.
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for two of them rather than one tree, flanking the ramp entrances of the Space Centre. In late March and April they flower before a single leaf appears.

trees.story:
Vancouver's heritage register is mostly buildings. It also keeps a category for landscape resources, and one entry on it is a single beech standing on the boulevard outside 1711 Dunbar Street.

Two separate arms of the same city have looked at that tree and agree on it. The heritage register calls it a beech and stops there. The street-tree inventory, a survey run for asset management rather than for history, records one European beech at the identical address: 133.4 centimetres of trunk diameter, which is about 4.2 metres round, and 19.8 metres of height. It lists no other tree at the address, so there is no question which one carries the listing.

Four metres of girth is well beyond the usual run of urban beech, which spend their lives with their roots under pavement. This one does too, on a quiet residential street in Kitsilano, on public ground, free to walk up to at any hour. Come in late October or November and the whole crown goes copper and russet.

What nobody has written down is its age. Neither dataset records a planting date and no independent account of the tree exists, and we would rather leave the field empty than fit a number to the girth without a growth rate we trust for beech on this coast. If you know when Dunbar Street got its beech, tell us.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the crown turns copper and russet

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the smooth grey beech trunk, 4.2 metres round and 19.8 metres tall. It is the only tree the city records standing on the boulevard outside 1711 Dunbar Street.

trees.access: Free. Public boulevard tree on the City of Vancouver street right-of-way, reachable and viewable from the public sidewalk at any time.
trees.transport: Residential street in Arbutus Ridge on Vancouver's west side; nearest bus service runs along nearby arterials (Arbutus Street or West King Edward Avenue), a short walk away.
trees.story:
There are two Spanish chestnuts on West 20th Avenue, and the heritage-listed one is the smaller. The city's street-tree inventory gives it a trunk 104.1 centimetres in diameter, about 3.3 metres round, and 19.8 metres of height; the unlisted chestnut a block away at number 2089 is thicker, at 124.5 centimetres. Fame and girth do not always travel together.

The city cannot quite agree where the listed one lives. Its heritage register records a Spanish Chestnut at 2001 West 20th Avenue. Its separate street-tree survey records a Spanish chestnut at 2003, one house number along, and finds no other chestnut at this end of the block. Almost certainly the same tree, counted twice by two departments working from two sets of paperwork. Almost certainly is the honest phrase: this pass could not settle it on the ground.

Castanea sativa is the sweet chestnut of Europe, which Vancouver's register files under its other name. This one grows on a city boulevard on the public right-of-way, free to walk up to at any hour. In October the spiny burs split and the nuts come down, which is the moment worth timing the walk for.

Nobody has recorded its age. Neither city dataset carries a planting date and no independent account of the tree turned up. If you have lived on the block long enough to know, tell us.

best_time.label: October, when the spiny burs split and the chestnuts come down

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long saw-toothed chestnut leaves and a trunk 3.3 metres round, on the boulevard outside 2003 West 20th Avenue. The street's other chestnut, a block away at 2089, is thicker.

verified_sources: City of Vancouver Heritage Register, category 'LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees', heritage_register_id 2535, common name 'Pin Oak', 4010 BLENHEIM ST, municipaldesignationm=No, dateoflastupdate 2020-10-14 (opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/heritage-sites/)

trees.access: Free. Public boulevard trees on the City of Vancouver street right-of-way, reachable and viewable from the public sidewalk at any time.
trees.transport: Residential street in Dunbar-Southlands on Vancouver's west side; nearest bus service runs along West 41st Avenue or Dunbar Street, several minutes' walk.
trees.story:
Vancouver's heritage register lists a pin oak at 4010 Blenheim Street. Vancouver's street-tree inventory, run by another department for another purpose, records no pin oak at 4010 Blenheim Street at all. What it records is five trees sharing that one civic address: two red oaks, two American elms and a young hackberry.

The tree on this page is the larger of the two red oaks, 127 centimetres in diameter, about 4 metres round, and 19.8 metres tall. Four metres of oak is a serious tree on a residential boulevard whichever species it turns out to be, and it is the likeliest candidate for the heritage listing: pin oak and red oak are both lobed red oaks and are confused constantly, in registers as much as in gardens.

The other possibility is that the register's pin oak stands on the private frontage of the lot, where the street-tree survey does not go, and that the tree we are pointing you at is its unlisted neighbour. Neither dataset settles it. If you know the block and can say which oak is which, tell us, because you can answer that from the pavement in about ten seconds and we cannot answer it from here at all.

No planting date or age is recorded for any of the five trees at the address, so the years this one has been standing there are nobody's number yet.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the thicker but shorter of the two red oaks at 4010 Blenheim Street: 4 metres round and 19.8 metres tall, against the neighbouring oak's 3.5 metres and 22.9.
